name: HCG (Human Chorionic Gonadotropin)

b.x: HCG (human chorionic gonadotropin, CAS 9002-61-3) is a 36.7 kDa glycoprotein produced naturally during pregnancy that binds the same receptor as LH on Leydig cells. Coviello and colleagues settled the dose question in 2005 [1]: at 250 IU every other day, intratesticular testosterone dropped only 7% from baseline; at 500 IU EOD, it climbed 26% above baseline. Without HCG, intratesticular testosterone fell to near zero. It binds the same receptor as LH on Leydig cells, triggering testosterone synthesis through the cAMP signaling cascade. Think of it as a long-acting LH substitute that bypasses the pituitary entirely. In practice, HCG sits at the center of two worlds. Fertility clinics use it under FDA-labeled indications for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. TRT clinics prescribe it off-label to prevent testicular atrophy and maintain sperm production in men on exogenous testosterone. The community protocols at 250 to 500 IU every other day line up precisely with the published dose-response data. The regulatory situation changed sharply in March 2020. On March 23, 2020, approved HCG applications were deemed biologics licenses under the BPCIA (FDA's deemed-BLA list). Brand-name Pregnyl or Novarel now runs about $289 per 10,000 IU vial at a discounted cash price, up from $20 to $40 when compounded versions were available. That cost shift pushed many US telehealth clinics toward gonadorelin as a compounded substitute, though no direct RCT proves gonadorelin matches HCG for intratesticular testosterone maintenance.

HCG binds to the LH/CG receptor (LHCGR) on Leydig cells in the testes. That receptor activation triggers the cAMP second messenger cascade, which drives cholesterol into the steroidogenic pathway and produces testosterone. The same receptor sits on Sertoli cells indirectly supporting spermatogenesis through paracrine signaling. What makes HCG useful during TRT is its ability to bypass the hypothalamic-pituitary axis completely. Exogenous testosterone shuts down the brain's GnRH pulse generator, which stops LH secretion. Leydig cells lose their signal, shrink, and stop producing testosterone locally. HCG replaces that missing LH signal at the gonadal level. The glycoprotein's molecular weight (36.7 kDa) gives it a half-life of roughly 33 hours, confirmed by the Pregnyl FDA label and Rizkallah's pharmacokinetic work. Endogenous LH has a half-life of about 20 minutes. That difference is why 250 to 500 IU every other day provides steady Leydig cell stimulation; you don't need continuous infusion or daily dosing. Subcutaneous bioavailability sits around 95%, clinically equivalent to intramuscular injection. Peak levels arrive at approximately 12 to 20 hours after subcutaneous administration. One limitation: HCG does not directly stimulate FSH receptors. Sertoli cell function depends on both testosterone (provided by HCG-stimulated Leydig cells) and FSH. In severe hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, HCG monotherapy produces sperm in about 78% of men, but adding exogenous FSH pushes outcomes higher (41 studies, n=1,673) [2].
HCG benefits center on testicular preservation, fertility maintenance, and hormonal support during testosterone replacement therapy.
Preserves intratesticular testosterone at 93% of baseline on just 250 IU every other day, per the Coviello 2005 dose-response study (n=29) [1].
Prevents testicular atrophy, the most consistently reported benefit across more than 2,000 threads on r/trt and r/Testosterone.
Maintains sperm production during TRT. Hsieh 2013 [3] tracked 26 men on concurrent TRT and 500 IU HCG every other day; zero developed azoospermia, and 9 achieved pregnancy.
FDA-approved with decades of clinical data supporting its safety profile, unlike most peptides on the market.
Real-world 2025 cohort data [4] confirmed 84 to 89% of anabolic steroid users showed sperm count improvement on similar HCG protocols, with median counts climbing from 18 million to 147 million.
Supports the full hormone cascade as an LH mimetic, maintaining downstream metabolites like estradiol that contribute to mood and sexual function.
Aligned
Scientific Evidence
Based on 10 key studies · FDA-approved
Strong evidence that HCG maintains intratesticular testosterone (ITT) during exogenous testosterone use and preserves spermatogenesis.
Dosing studied: 250-500 IU every other day (EOD) SC for TRT adjunct; 500-1,500 IU 3x/week SC for PCT; 500-1,000 IU 3x/week IM for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (FDA label)

Dose-response established: 250 IU EOD maintains ITT at ~93% of baseline; 500 IU EOD brings ITT ~26% above baseline. HCG + FSH combination superior to HCG monotherapy for restoring spermatogenesis in severe hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. FDA-approved for fertility indications with decades of clinical data.
Key Study
Coviello et al. 2005 (PMID 15713727): ITT dose-response in men on 200 mg/week testosterone enanthate; n=29. Confirmed: 250 IU EOD = -7% ITT vs baseline; 500 IU EOD = +26% ITT above baseline.
Limitations

Most TRT-adjunct ITT data from small trials. No large RCT comparing HCG to gonadorelin for ITT maintenance in TRT patients. Long-term Leydig desensitization threshold (>1,500 IU/injection) based on animal data and clinical inference, not prospective human RCT.
Community Experience
Widely regarded as the gold standard for testicular preservation and fertility maintenance on TRT.
Community dosing: 250-500 IU EOD SC is the dominant community standard; 500-1,000 IU 3x/week for active fertility; 1,500 IU 3x/week for PCT blast phase

Community protocols closely mirror clinical data. Cost and availability since the March 2020 BPCIA transition are the dominant barriers; gonadorelin has largely replaced compounded HCG at US telehealth clinics.

Science & Community Aligned

Community protocols at 250-500 IU EOD precisely match the Coviello 2005 dose-response data. PCT protocols align with 2026 clinical cohort data (PMID 41147237). No significant divergence between science and community on dosing or indication.

Community TRT community standard: 250-500 IU SC every other day (r/trt, r/Testosterone). The aggressive tier, 1,000 IU 3x/week, sits inside the Pregnyl label range for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (500-1,000 USP units 3x/week). [Source](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2023/017692s028s036s043lbl.pdf)

Reconstitution math for a 5,000 IU vial with 2 mL bacteriostatic water: you get 2,500 IU per mL, or 250 IU per 10 units on a standard 100-unit insulin syringe. For 500 IU, draw to the 20-unit mark. For 1,500 IU (PCT dosing), that's 60 units. Always use bacteriostatic water, not sterile water. Multi-dose vials need the benzyl alcohol preservative. Sterile water accelerates degradation fast after reconstitution. Store reconstituted HCG refrigerated at 2 to 8 degrees Celsius and use within 60 days per the Pregnyl label. Lyophilized powder keeps at room temperature for up to 60 days or refrigerated for up to 2 years. The thing most beginners miss: since March 23, 2020, FDA says HCG is not eligible for the 503A/503B compounding exemptions. If a telehealth clinic offers "compounded HCG," that product falls outside both exemptions. The discounted cash price for Pregnyl 10,000 IU runs roughly $289 at retail pharmacies. Check the NDC number on your vial to confirm it matches the Organon or Ferring product.
Cycling
Typically used continuously alongside TRT, not cycled. For PCT, 2-4 weeks is common. Doses above 1,500 IU per injection risk Leydig cell desensitization.
HCG (Human Chorionic Gonadotropin)

For TRT adjunct use, HCG is administered continuously at doses ≤500 IU EOD to avoid Leydig cell LHCGR downregulation. Doses >1,500 IU per injection risk chronic receptor desensitization, reducing responsiveness over time. PCT use is inherently time-limited (2-4 months): the protocol self-terminates when spermatogenesis is restored. No formal "cycling on/off" schedule is indicated for continuous low-dose TRT adjunct use.
Declining testicular volume despite continued HCG use at stable dose (possible receptor downregulation)
Loss of prior E2 elevation on same dose (reduced steroidogenic Leydig cell response)
Worsening libido or mood symptoms not explained by TRT dose changes

Alternative Routes
Subcutaneous (SC)
No dose adjustment: SC bioavailability ~95%, clinically equivalent to IM

More comfortable; easier to self-administer; less post-injection soreness. Abdominal fat, thigh, or upper arm acceptable sites. Tmax slightly delayed vs IM (~12 hours SC vs ~6 hours IM per Pregnyl label), not clinically relevant for EOD or 3x/week TRT dosing. Use 29-31G insulin syringe, 4-8mm needle.
Intramuscular (IM)
Same dose as SC; no adjustment needed

FDA label specifies IM for all labeled indications. Tmax ~6 hours IM per Pregnyl label. More painful than SC. Deltoid or gluteal sites. More common in clinical fertility protocols; SC broadly substituted in TRT practice.
Works With
Gonadorelin

HCG has not been eligible for the 503A/503B compounding exemptions since March 2020 (FDA). Gonadorelin has largely replaced compounded HCG at US TRT clinics as a compounded LH-stimulating alternative. Acts at pituitary level (vs HCG at gonadal level); stimulates both LH and FSH. Some clinics run both: brand-name HCG for proven ITT maintenance + gonadorelin to maintain pituitary axis stimulation.
Gonadorelin 100-200 mcg SC 2x/day (compounded) or pulsatile 50-100 mcg every 90 min (pump). Typically used as HCG substitute, not simultaneous addition.
Kisspeptin-10

Upstream HPG axis stimulator. Not a practical HCG alternative while on TRT: exogenous testosterone suppresses kisspeptin signaling at hypothalamic level, blunting efficacy. Potentially useful during post-TRT HPG axis recovery phase. Very limited human male data as of 2025; FDA PCAC nominated for TRT spermatogenesis indication (Oct 2024) but not yet approved for compounding.
Avoid
GnRH agonists (leuprolide, buserelin, triptorelin): continuous use

Continuous GnRH agonist use causes LH/FSH suppression via pituitary receptor downregulation, directly opposing HCG's LH-mimetic effect on Leydig cells. Combination is physiologically counterproductive.
GnRH antagonists (cetrorelix, ganirelix)

Blocks pituitary GnRH receptors, suppressing endogenous LH/FSH. While HCG bypasses the pituitary, combining with GnRH antagonists creates unpredictable hormonal disruption without clear therapeutic rationale outside closely supervised fertility protocols.
Brand Price

Pregnyl 10,000 IU: ~$289 discounted cash price / ~$427-$465 retail (Organon). Novarel 10,000 IU: ~$289 discounted cash price / ~$432 retail (Ferring). Ovidrel 250 mcg prefilled syringe: ~$107-$235 discounted cash price (single-use fertility trigger format: not suitable for TRT EOD protocols).
Compounded

Not eligible for the 503A/503B compounding exemptions since March 23, 2020, when HCG became a licensed biologic (FDA notice to compounders). Gonadorelin (~$30-50/month compounded) is the common domestic substitute.
Pricing updated 2026-04-09

Raised estradiol is the primary management challenge with HCG. The mechanism is straightforward: HCG stimulates Leydig cells to produce testosterone, and aromatase converts a portion of that testosterone to estradiol. Men with higher body fat or genetic aromatase polymorphisms are more susceptible. At 250 IU every other day, most men manage without an aromatase inhibitor. At 500 IU and above, symptomatic estradiol elevation becomes common enough that labs at 4 to 6 weeks are standard practice. Water retention and bloating follow from estradiol elevation and tend to appear at moderate to high doses. Gynecomastia risk exists if estrogen climbs unchecked, particularly in men already prone to breast tissue sensitivity. Nipple tenderness or puffiness warrants bloodwork, not panic. Leydig cell desensitization is the risk that gets less attention but matters most over time. Chronic dosing above 1,500 IU per injection can downregulate LHCGR expression on Leydig cells, reducing their responsiveness to both HCG and endogenous LH. This threshold comes from animal data and clinical inference rather than a prospective human RCT, but it's the reason every experienced protocol caps individual injections at 1,500 IU. Signs include declining testicular volume despite continued use and loss of the estradiol elevation you'd expect at a given dose. Injection site reactions are typical for both intramuscular and subcutaneous administration. Pain, redness, and mild swelling at the injection site affect a subset of users. Rotating sites and using 29 to 31 gauge insulin needles minimizes discomfort. Acne and oily skin show up in community reports at doses above 500 IU, consistent with the higher intratesticular testosterone production at those levels. Headache and irritability appear in clinical literature and user reports without a clear dose-response pattern. Not everyone responds to HCG for fertility. Some men remain azoospermic despite adequate dosing; HCG targets Leydig cells but doesn't directly stimulate Sertoli cells. FSH addition is the standard next step for non-responders [2]. When to stop or seek medical evaluation: persistent gynecomastia symptoms, hematocrit above 52%, signs of Leydig desensitization (declining response at stable dose), or any allergic reaction. Contraindicated in hormone-sensitive cancers (prostate, breast), precocious puberty, and pregnancy unless under direct fertility specialist supervision.
Common Issues & Solutions

Estradiol rising after HCG: HCG drives Leydig cell testosterone production, which aromatizes to E2. Test E2 at 4-6 weeks; add anastrozole 0.25-0.5 mg or exemestane 12.5 mg on injection days only if confirmed elevated and symptomatic. Do not add AI preemptively without labs.

Testicular volume not recovering after 3 months: Increase from 250 IU to 500 IU EOD. For active fertility, 500 IU EOD is the minimum evidence-backed dose (Hsieh 2013). If still insufficient at 6 months, add FSH (Gonal-F or Follistim): HCG drives testosterone but FSH is required for full Sertoli cell support and spermatogenesis.

Azoospermia persisting despite HCG: HCG targets Leydig cells (testosterone) but not Sertoli cells directly. FSH is required for full spermatogenesis. Add FSH stimulation per specialist; PMID 39445789 meta-analysis confirms HCG + FSH combination superior to HCG alone for sperm output in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

Cost and supply since March 23, 2020: HCG is not eligible for the 503A/503B compounding exemptions (FDA). Brand-name Pregnyl/Novarel ~$289 discounted cash price. Consider gonadorelin (compounded, ~$30-50/month) as a cost-accessible alternative: note no direct RCT proving ITT equivalence to HCG for TRT adjunct.

Using sterile water instead of bacteriostatic water: Multi-dose vials require bacteriostatic water (0.9% benzyl alcohol preservative). Sterile water has no preservative and significantly accelerates degradation after reconstitution. Always use bac water for HCG vials.

HCG is FDA-approved under brand names Pregnyl (Organon), Novarel (Ferring), and Ovidrel (EMD Serono) for fertility indications including hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and ovulation induction. HCG is a prescription-only drug, and its use alongside TRT is off-label. The critical regulatory change happened on March 23, 2020. Under the Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act (BPCIA), approved HCG applications became biologics licenses that day (FDA's deemed-BLA list). FDA's notice to compounders names human chorionic gonadotropin among the affected substances. It says these transitioning biological products are not eligible for the 503A and 503B compounding exemptions. Product sold in the US as "compounded HCG" since then falls outside both exemptions and may be mislabeled or counterfeit. FDA-licensed HCG (Pregnyl, Novarel, Ovidrel and a Fresenius Kabi chorionic gonadotropin) is dispensed by prescription. Imported HCG (Canada, Mexico) raises cold-chain and quality verification concerns. HCG is banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) at all times for male athletes under the S2 category (peptide hormones, growth factors, and related substances). A positive test results in a sanction. This content is for educational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Consult a licensed healthcare provider before using any prescription medication.

faqs.q: Why does HCG cause elevated estrogen, and do I need an AI?
faqs.a: HCG stimulates Leydig cells to produce testosterone, and some of that testosterone converts to estradiol via aromatase; same pathway as exogenous testosterone. At doses of 250-500 IU every other day, many men manage fine without an aromatase inhibitor. If you carry more body fat or have genetic factors that increase aromatase activity, low-dose anastrozole (0.25-0.5 mg) may help. Always test estradiol before automatically adding an AI.

faqs.q: What is the recommended HCG (Human Chorionic Gonadotropin) dosage?
faqs.a: HCG (Human Chorionic Gonadotropin) dosing varies by experience level. Beginners typically start at 250 IU eod, moderate users at 500 IU eod, and aggressive protocols use 1,000 IU 3x/week.

faqs.q: How do you reconstitute HCG (Human Chorionic Gonadotropin)?
faqs.a: HCG (Human Chorionic Gonadotropin) typically comes in 5000IU or 10000IU vials. Add 2mL of bacteriostatic water to the vial. Use the free calculator for exact syringe units based on your desired dose.

faqs.q: What is the half-life of HCG (Human Chorionic Gonadotropin)?
faqs.a: The half-life of HCG (Human Chorionic Gonadotropin) is ~33 hours. This determines how frequently you need to dose for consistent blood levels.

summary: . HCG is a glycoprotein hormone that mimics luteinizing hormone, and it's become the standard tool for preserving testicular function on TRT. The FDA approved it decades ago under brand names Pregnyl, Novarel, and Ovidrel. One complication: compounding pharmacies lost the right to produce HCG in March 2020 after BPCIA reclassification, pushing costs from $20 to $289 or more per vial. Men on testosterone replacement still reach for it because nothing else matches the evidence for preventing atrophy and protecting fertility.
